items.title: Q1 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which statement among the following rightly defines an 'epithet'?
options: An adjective/adjectival phrase that condemns the protagonist of a story/novel
An adjective/adjectival phrase used to define a characteristic quality or attribute of some person or thing
An adjective/adjectival phrase suited for inscription on a tomb or memorial
A rhetorical figure by which the same word or phrase is repeated at the end of successive lines
items.explanation: An epithet is an adjective or adjectival phrase used to characterize a distinct quality or attribute of a person or thing, such as Homer's 'swift-footed Achilles' or 'rosy-fingered dawn'.

items.title: Q2 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit II: Poetry · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.stem: Who among the following invented 'inscape' and 'instress'?
items.explanation: Victorian poet Gerard Manley Hopkins coined the terms 'inscape' (the unique, individualizing design or inner essence of a natural thing) and 'instress' (the divine energy that sustains an inscape and transmits it to the perceiver).

items.title: Q3 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: A 'palindrome' is __________.
options: A recantation in song or verse
A play on words by alteration of letters.
A word or sentence which reads the same both ways.
A sequence of clauses or sentences which have a symmetrical structure.
items.explanation: A palindrome is a word or sentence that reads the same forwards and backwards, like 'madam' or 'level'.

items.title: Q4 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Jean-François Lyotard
items.stem: In his work, The Postmodern Condition, Jean Francois Lyotard announced the eclipse of all grand narratives and sought to declare the death of
items.explanation: In The Postmodern Condition: A Report on Knowledge (1979), Jean-Francois Lyotard defined postmodernism as 'incredulity toward metanarratives,' announcing the eclipse of Enlightenment grand narratives and the demise of Classical Socialism (orthodox Marxism).

items.title: Q5 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: What was the name of the first ship to transport indentured labourers from India to Trinidad and Tobago in 1845?
items.explanation: The Fatel Razack (spelled 'Futtle Rozack' in colonial shipping records) was the first vessel to transport Indian indentured labourers from Calcutta to Trinidad and Tobago, arriving in Port of Spain on 30 May 1845.

items.title: Q6 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit II: Poetry · John Milton
items.stem: Who among the following was known as 'The Lady of Christ's' during his college days at Cambridge?
items.explanation: John Milton was nicknamed 'The Lady of Christ's' by his fellow students at Christ's College, Cambridge, on account of his fair complexion, delicate features, and strict moral rectitude.

items.title: Q7 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas Browne
items.stem: Sir Thomas Browne's longest work, Vulgar Errors, is about
options: the mistaken beliefs of the poorly educated
vulgar beliefs and practices of the time
use of vulgar language in literary works
items.explanation: Sir Thomas Browne's Pseudodoxia Epidemica, or Vulgar Errors (1646), is an encyclopedic work of seventeenth-century prose that refutes common superstitions, folklore, and mistaken beliefs held by the unlearned public ('the vulgar').

items.title: Q8 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit I: Drama · Thomas Norton, Thomas Sackville
items.stem: The first regular English tragedy Gorboduc contains 5 acts; while the first 3 acts were written by Thomas Norton, identify the author who wrote the remaining 2 acts
items.explanation: In Gorboduc (1561), the first regular five-act English tragedy in blank verse, the first three acts were written by Thomas Norton and the final two acts were composed by Thomas Sackville.

items.title: Q9 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early Tudor & Humanist Reformation · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · William Tyndale
items.stem: Who among the following English translators of the Bible was burnt to death for his beliefs, however, he is remembered for his careful and important work on translation?
items.explanation: Protestant reformer William Tyndale produced the first English New Testament translated directly from Greek and Hebrew manuscripts (1525–26). Arrested for heresy, he was strangled and burned at the stake in Vilvoorde in 1536, though his phrasing shaped the King James Bible.

items.title: Q10 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit II: Poetry · Edmund Spenser
items.stem: How many Knights feature in Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene?
items.explanation: Spenser planned twelve books of The Faerie Queene, each with one knight showing a virtue. So twelve knights feature in the plan, though only six books were finished.

items.title: Q11 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · Unit II: Poetry · Alexander Pope
items.stem: Alexander Pope's famous quote, "A little knowledge is a dangerous thing," appears in which one of the following works?
items.explanation: The famous proverb 'A little learning [often misquoted as knowledge] is a dangerous thing; / Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring' appears in Part II of Alexander Pope's verse essay An Essay on Criticism (1711).

items.title: Q12 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: 15th-Century Transition, Drama & Early Print · Unit I: Drama · Anonymous — Everyman
items.stem: Who among the following friends of Everyman, the main protagonist of the best-known Morality play, Everyman, stays with him when he leaves the world to face Death?
items.explanation: In the late-fifteenth-century morality play Everyman, worldly companions such as Fellowship, Kindred, Goods, Beauty, Strength, and even Knowledge desert Everyman at the grave's edge, and only Good Deeds accompanies him before God.

items.title: Q13 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: Which of the following citations of an article published in a journal is in the correct format according to MLA Handbook (9th Edition)?
options: 2016. Boggs, Colleen Glenney. "Public Reading and the Civil War Draft Lottery." American Periodicals, vol. 26, no. 2, 2016, pp. 149-66
"Public Reading and the Civil War Draft Lottery." American Periodicals, vol. 26, no. 2, 2016, P. 149-66.
Boggs, Colleen Glenney, American Periodicals. "Public Reading and the Civil War Draft Lottery." vol. 26, no. 2, 2016, P. 149-66
Boggs, Colleen Glenney. "Public Reading and the Civil War Draft Lottery." American Periodicals, vol. 26, no. 2, 2016, pp. 149-66.
items.explanation: MLA 9 style gives the author's name first, then the article title in quotation marks, then the journal title in italics, then volume, number, year and pages (pp.). Only option 4 follows this order.

items.title: Q14 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: While documenting, when is a block quotation used in prose?
options: If a quotation runs in more than four lines
If a quotation runs in more than five lines
If a quotation runs in more than three lines
If a quotation runs in more than two lines
items.explanation: According to the MLA Handbook (8th and 9th editions), a prose quotation that runs to more than four lines in the writer's text must be set off from the main text as an indented block quotation without quotation marks.

items.title: Q15 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: How the words from a language other than English are written in a research paper?
items.explanation: In academic style guides including the MLA Handbook, words and phrases from a language other than English that have not been naturalized into English are formatted in italics.

items.title: Q16 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: According to MLA Handbook, the mechanics of prose refers to technical questions that writers must follow. These include
options: Spelling, punctuation, capitalization, style of numbering
Spelling, capitalization, style of numbering, linguistics
items.explanation: In the MLA Handbook, 'the mechanics of prose' (also titled 'The Mechanics of Writing') covers technical conventions of presentation including spelling, punctuation, capitalization, italics, names, and the style of numbers/numbering.

items.title: Q17 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · John Crowe Ransom
items.stem: Who among the following published a series of essays titled The New Criticism?
items.explanation: American poet and critic John Crowe Ransom published The New Criticism in 1941, a collection of essays examining I. A. Richards, T. S. Eliot, and Yvor Winters that gave the New Criticism movement its name.

items.title: Q18 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: Who among the following observed that "the artistic critic, like the mystic, is an antimonium always?"
items.explanation: Oscar Wilde made this observation in his dialogue essay 'The Critic as Artist' (included in Intentions, 1891), where Gilbert remarks, 'For the artistic critic, like the mystic, is an antinomian always.'

items.title: Q19 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Blake, Robert Southey
items.stem: Who among the following was not associated with Lake School of Poetry?
items.explanation: The 'Lake School' (or Lake Poets) was a label applied by Francis Jeffrey in the Edinburgh Review to William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, and Robert Southey, who lived in the Lake District. London-based visionary poet William Blake was never part of this group.

items.title: Q20 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · J. B. Priestley, Kingsley Amis, John Osborne, Colin Wilson
items.stem: Who among the following did not belong to 'Angry Young Men' generation of British playwrights/novelists?
items.explanation: J. B. Priestley (1894–1984) belonged to an earlier generation of twentieth-century British dramatists known for An Inspector Calls (1945), whereas Kingsley Amis, John Osborne, and Colin Wilson were leading figures of the 1950s 'Angry Young Men' generation.

items.title: Q21 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · May Sinclair
items.stem: Who among the following coined the term 'Stream of Consciousness'?
items.explanation: While philosopher William James coined the phrase in Principles of Psychology (1890), novelist and critic May Sinclair was the first to apply 'stream of consciousness' to literature in her April 1918 review of Dorothy Richardson's Pointed Roofs in The Egoist.

items.title: Q22 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Jean Rhys
items.stem: Which among the following is not a novel written by Jean Rhys?
items.explanation: Quartet (1928), Voyage in the Dark (1934), and Good Morning, Midnight (1939) are modernist novels by Dominican-born writer Jean Rhys, whereas Golden Child (2019) is a debut novel by Trinidadian author Claire Adam.

items.title: Q23 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Mary Wollstonecraft
items.stem: What is the title of Mary Wollstonecraft's autobiographical novel?
options: Maria; or, the Wrongs of Woman
items.explanation: Mary Wollstonecraft's debut novel Mary: A Fiction (1788) is a semi-autobiographical work inspired by her intense attachment to her close friend Fanny Blood.

items.title: Q24 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Louisa May Alcott
items.stem: Which text among the following is the sequel to Louisa Mary Alcott's novel, Little Women?
items.explanation: Good Wives (1869) is the immediate sequel (originally published as Part Second) to Louisa May Alcott's Little Women (1868), following the March sisters into marriage and adulthood prior to Little Men (1871) and Jo's Boys (1886).

items.title: Q25 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Maya Angelou
items.stem: Who among the following is the author of I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings?
items.explanation: American poet and civil rights activist Maya Angelou wrote the acclaimed 1969 autobiography I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, chronicling her early years in Stamps, Arkansas.

items.title: Q26 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Wolfgang Iser
items.stem: Who among the following is the author of The Implied Reader and The Act of Reading?
items.explanation: German reader-response theorist Wolfgang Iser, a leading figure of the Constance School of reception aesthetics, authored The Implied Reader (1972; trans. 1974) and The Act of Reading: A Theory of Aesthetic Response (1976; trans. 1978).

items.title: Q27 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Jacques Lacan
items.stem: Which among the following is not a state of human mental disposition as posited by Jacques Lacan?
items.explanation: French psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan structured human subjectivity around three interconnected registers—the Imaginary, the Symbolic, and the Real. 'The Historical Order' is not part of Lacan's triad.

items.title: Q28 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · George Eliot
items.stem: Which among the following novelists remarked that "falsehood is so easy, truth so difficult... Examine your words well, and you will find that even when you have no motive to be false, it is a very hard thing to say the exact truth, even about your own immediate feelings?"
items.explanation: This famous reflection on literary realism and the difficulty of telling the exact truth appears in Chapter 17 ('In Which the Story Pauses a Little') of George Eliot's novel Adam Bede (1859).

items.title: Q29 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.stem: Who among the following stated that "true philosopher and the true poet are one, and a beauty, which is truth, and a truth, which is beauty, is the aim of both?"
items.explanation: American Transcendentalist Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote in Chapter VI ('Idealism') of his foundational essay Nature (1836): 'The true philosopher and the true poet are one, and a beauty, which is truth, and a truth, which is beauty, is the aim of both.'

items.title: Q30 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Joseph Addison, Richard Steele
items.stem: Which periodical was started by Joseph Addison and Richard Steele after closing of the Spectator in 1712?
items.explanation: After the original run of The Spectator ended in December 1712, Richard Steele—with frequent contributions from Joseph Addison—launched the daily periodical The Guardian, which ran from March to October 1713.

items.title: Q31 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · John Dryden, Samuel Johnson
items.stem: Who among the following called John Dryden as the father of English Criticism and affirmed that modern English prose began with Dryden's Essay of Dramatic Poesy?
items.explanation: In his 'Life of Dryden' (from Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets, 1779–81), Samuel Johnson hailed John Dryden as 'the father of English criticism,' praising An Essay of Dramatic Poesy as the model of modern English critical prose.

items.title: Q32 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Virginia Woolf, John Maynard Keynes, Lytton Strachey, Edmund Husserl
items.stem: Who among the following was not associated with Bloomsbury Group?
items.explanation: Virginia Woolf, economist John Maynard Keynes, and biographer Lytton Strachey were core members of the London-based Bloomsbury Group, whereas Edmund Husserl (1859–1938) was the German philosopher who founded phenomenology.

items.title: Q33 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Roman Jakobson
items.stem: Which among the following critics stated that, "The object of study in literary science is not literature but 'Literariness', that is, what makes a given work a literary work?"
items.explanation: Russian Formalist critic and linguist Roman Jakobson famously declared in Modern Russian Poetry (1921) that 'The object of study in literary science is not literature, but "literariness" (literaturnost), that is, what makes a given work a literary work.'

items.title: Q34 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Philip Sidney, Stephen Gosson
items.stem: What was the immediate motivation for Philip Sidney to write Apologie for Poetrie as a defense of poetry?
options: Emphasis on history in Holinshed's Chronicles
Philosophical questions raised in Thomas More's Utopia
Attack on poetry in The School of Abuse by Stephen Gosson
Exposure of human foibles and failings in Erasmus's In Praise of Folly
items.explanation: Sir Philip Sidney was directly provoked to write An Apologie for Poetrie (composed c. 1579–80, published 1595) by Puritan pamphleteer Stephen Gosson, who had dedicated his invective against poets and playwrights, The Schoole of Abuse (1579), to Sidney without permission.

items.title: Q35 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · Samuel Taylor Coleridge
items.stem: The poem "France: An Ode" is written by
items.explanation: Samuel Taylor Coleridge wrote 'France: An Ode' (originally published as 'The Recantation: An Ode' in the Morning Post in April 1798) after revolutionary France invaded Switzerland, expressing his disillusionment with French military aggression.

items.title: Q36 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Joseph Addison
items.stem: Who among the following defined taste as "that faculty of the soul, which discerns the beauties of an author with pleasure, and the imperfections with dislike?"
items.explanation: In The Spectator, No. 409 (June 19, 1712), Joseph Addison defined literary taste as 'that Faculty of the Soul, which discerns the Beauties of an Author with Pleasure, and the Imperfections with Dislike.'

items.title: Q37 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth
items.stem: The poetic line(s), "There is one great society alone on earth: the noble living and the noble dead" appear in
items.explanation: The lines 'There is / One great society alone on earth: / The noble Living and the noble Dead' appear in Book XI ('France, Concluded') of William Wordsworth's autobiographical epic poem The Prelude.

items.title: Q38 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: What does 'an eponymous' character mean?
options: An eponymous character is essentially devilish in nature
An eponymous character gives his or her name to the title of the work
An eponymous character is intriguing in nature
An eponymous character is superfluous in the plot
items.explanation: An eponymous character (from the Greek eponymos, 'giving one's name to') is a character whose name also serves as the title of the literary work, such as Robinson Crusoe, Jane Eyre, or Hamlet.

items.title: Q39 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit I: Drama · Eugene O'Neill, Sean O'Casey
items.stem: Which among the following is not a play written by Eugene O'Neill?
items.explanation: The Plough and the Stars (1926), set during the 1916 Easter Rising in Dublin, was written by Irish dramatist Sean O'Casey. Anna Christie (1921), All God's Chillun Got Wings (1924), and Strange Interlude (1928) are plays by American playwright Eugene O'Neill.

items.title: Q40 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which statement among the following rightly defines 'an invective'?
options: Denunciatory, abusive or vituperative speech or writing
Eulogising speech, writing or act of a person
Speech or writing that establishes the belief in God
Speech or writing that is essentially appreciative of a person
items.explanation: An invective is denunciatory, abusive, or vituperative speech or writing that attacks, insults, or rails against a person, institution, or opinion.

items.title: Q41 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Raymond Williams
items.stem:
Arrange the following works of Raymond Williams in the correct chronological order of their publication -
A. Keywords
B. Culture and Society
C. The Long Revolution
D. The Country and the City
E. Modern Tragedy
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The chronological order of Raymond Williams's major books is: Culture and Society (B, 1958), The Long Revolution (C, 1961), Modern Tragedy (E, 1966), The Country and the City (D, 1973), and Keywords (A, 1976), giving B, C, E, D, A.

items.title: Q42 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit VI: English in India · B. R. Ambedkar
items.stem:
Arrange the following works of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar in the correct chronological order of their publication.
A. Mr. Gandhi and Emancipation of Untouchables
B. The Annihilation of Caste
C. The Problem of the Rupee: Its Origin and its Solution
D. Federation Versus Freedom
E. Buddha and his Dhamma
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The chronological order of Dr. B. R. Ambedkar's works is: The Problem of the Rupee (C, 1923), Annihilation of Caste (B, 1936), Federation Versus Freedom (D, 1939), Mr. Gandhi and the Emancipation of the Untouchables (A, 1943), and The Buddha and His Dhamma (E, 1957), giving C, B, D, A, E.

items.title: Q43 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Walter Benjamin, Mikhail Bakhtin, Simone de Beauvoir, Roland Barthes, Jean Baudrillard
items.stem:
Arrange the following philosophers/theorists in the correct chronological order of their birth-
A. Simone de Beauvoir
B. Walter Benjamin
C. Jean Baudrillard
D. Mikhail Bakhtin
E. Roland Barthes
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Ordered by birth year, the sequence of these theorists is: Walter Benjamin (B, 1892), Mikhail Bakhtin (D, 1895), Simone de Beauvoir (A, 1908), Roland Barthes (E, 1915), and Jean Baudrillard (C, 1929), matching B, D, A, E, C.

items.title: Q44 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit VI: English in India · Sri Aurobindo, Sarojini Naidu, K. S. Venkataramani, R. K. Narayan, Raja Rao
items.stem:
Arrange the following Indian writers in the correct chronological order of their birth-
A. R.K. Narayan
B. Raja Rao
C. Sri Aurobindo
D. K.S. Venkataramani
E. Sarojini Naidu
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Ordered by birth year, the sequence of these Indian English writers is: Sri Aurobindo (C, 1872), Sarojini Naidu (E, 1879), K. S. Venkataramani (D, 1891), R. K. Narayan (A, 1906), and Raja Rao (B, 1908), giving C, E, D, A, B.

items.title: Q45 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit VI: English in India · Raja Rao, Bhabani Bhattacharya, G. V. Desani, R. K. Narayan
items.stem:

A. So Many Hungers
B. All About H. Hatter
C. Music for Mohini
D. Waiting for the Mahatama
E. Kanthapura
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The chronological publication order of these Indian English novels is: Raja Rao's Kanthapura (E, 1938), Bhabani Bhattacharya's So Many Hungers! (A, 1947), G. V. Desani's All About H. Hatterr (B, 1948), Bhabani Bhattacharya's Music for Mohini (C, 1952), and R. K. Narayan's Waiting for the Mahatma (D, 1955), giving E, A, B, C, D.

items.title: Q46 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit I: Drama · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem:
Arrange the following plays of G.B. Shaw in the correct chronological order of their publication:
A. Pygmalion
B. Man and Superman
C. Arms and the Man
D. Too True to be Good
E. Saint Joan
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The chronological order of George Bernard Shaw's plays is: Arms and the Man (C, 1894), Man and Superman (B, 1903), Pygmalion (A, 1913), Saint Joan (E, 1923), and Too True to Be Good (D, 1932), giving C, B, A, E, D.

items.title: Q47 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Agatha Christie
items.stem:
Arrange the following detective novels of Agatha Christie in the correct chronological order of their publication.
A. Death on the Nile
B. Murder in the Orient Express
C. Sparkling Cyanide
D. The Mysterious Affair at Styles
E. The Murder of Roger Ackroyd
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The chronological publication sequence of Agatha Christie's detective novels is: The Mysterious Affair at Styles (D, 1920), The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (E, 1926), Murder on the Orient Express (B, 1934), Death on the Nile (A, 1937), and Sparkling Cyanide (C, 1945), matching D, E, B, A, C.

items.title: Q48 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · J. R. R. Tolkien, C. S. Lewis, William Golding, Philip Pullman, J. K. Rowling

A. J.K. Rowling - The Goblet of Fire
B. Philip Pullman - Northern Lights
C. C.S. Lewis- The Lion, The Witch, and the Wardrobe
D. J.R.R. Tolkien's - The Hobbit
E. William Golding's - Lord of the Flies
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Starting with J. R. R. Tolkien's The Hobbit (D, 1937), followed by mid-century classics Lord of the Flies (E, 1954) and The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe (C, 1950), Philip Pullman's Northern Lights (B, 1995), and J. K. Rowling's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (A, 2000), Option 1 (D, E, C, B, A) is the only choice matching the 1937 start and 1995–2000 end.

items.title: Q49 · Aug 2024 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India · Dhananjaya
items.stem:
According to Dhananjaya, there are five elements of the plot, parallel with the five stages of the action, from these respectively arise the five junctures (Samadhi). What is the correct sequence of these junctures?
A. Avamarsa
B. mukha
C. pratimukha
D. upasamhrti
E. gurbha
Choose the correct answer from the options given below

E. 'Dream Work' is a psychoanalytical term to describe the mechanism that transforms raw material of a dream to its manifest content.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Michel Foucault's 'biopolitics' examines how modern states rationalize problems of population management (B), Gerard Genette defines 'hypertext' in Palimpsestes as a second-degree text derived from an earlier 'hypotext' (C), and Sigmund Freud's 'dream-work' (Traumarbeit) transforms latent dream thoughts into manifest content (E). items.explanation: Bhavabhuti's Sanskrit play Uttararamacharita ('The Later Story of Rama') is based on the Ramayana (C), derives its plot from the Uttara Kanda or last canto of the epic (D), and structures its dramatic time-space across two broad movements of separation and reunion (A). Act I depicts Rama and Sita viewing painted scrolls of their past rather than Rama's childhood, and Sita finds refuge in Valmiki's hermitage rather than Visvamitra's; thus A, C, D only.

items.explanation: Vishnusharma's Panchatantra was composed as a niti-sastra manual to instruct a king's sons in statecraft and wise conduct (B), the Kashmiri Tantrakhyayika is one of its oldest surviving Sanskrit recensions (D), and it is divided into five tantras or books (E). B. Sir Thomas More was the first to apply 'Utopia' to literary genre when he named his imaginary republic Utopia
C. Thomas More's Utopia was originally written in English.
D. Orwell's Nineteen Eighty Four and Aldous Huxley's Brave New World are dystopian/anti-utopian texts.
E. More's Utopia was translated into French, German and Spanish by Ralph Robinson.

items.explanation: Sir Thomas More coined and applied 'Utopia' (Greek for 'no-place' / 'good-place') to his imaginary island republic in 1516 (B), and George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four and Aldous Huxley's Brave New World are canonical dystopian/anti-utopian novels (D). I believe implicitly that the child is not born mischievous in the bad sense of the term. If parents would behave themselves whilst the child is growing, before it is born and after, it is a well-known fact that the child would instinctively obey the law of truth and the law of love...

If we are to reach real peace in this world and if we are to carry on a real war against war, we shall have to begin with children; and if they will grow up in their natural innocence, we won't have to struggle, we won't have to pass fruitless, idle resolutions, but we shall go from love to love and peace to peace, until at last all the corners of the world are covered with that peace and love for which, consciously or unconsciously, the whole world is hungering.

To believe and spend time praying and following rituals properly.
To turn towards children in humility and innocence to learn wisdom.
items.explanation: In this passage (from Mahatma Gandhi's October 1931 speech at the Montessori Training College in London), the author precedes 'I believe and pass my time and endeavour to obey His will' by citing Jesus's teaching that wisdom comes out of the mouths of babes and urging adults to approach children in humility and innocence to learn wisdom.
